microtopics.title: Particle model, speed distributions and phase change
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must connect distributed molecular motion to macroscopic temperature and distinguish surface evaporation from pressure-dependent boiling.
entry_assumptions: Can read basic chemical symbols and distinguish a named model from an observation.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Temperature describes ensemble kinetic behaviour rather than one common molecular speed, while phase-change claims require the relevant pressure and equilibrium conditions.

teaching_path.action: Separate the microscopic particle model from the macroscopic observation.
teaching_path.why_valid: Bulk temperature and pressure summarize many-particle behaviour; one molecule is not the thermodynamic state.
teaching_path.output: Use distributions and averages when connecting molecular motion to temperature.

teaching_path.action: Compare evaporation with boiling before discussing temperature.
teaching_path.why_valid: Evaporation can occur at a surface over a range of temperatures; boiling is a bulk transition when vapour pressure matches external pressure.
teaching_path.output: A boiling temperature is pressure-dependent, whereas evaporation need not wait for that condition.

teaching_path.action: Track energy through a phase change for a pure substance at fixed pressure in phase equilibrium.
teaching_path.why_valid: Energy supplied during coexistence can change phase rather than raise temperature.
teaching_path.output: Latent heat is energy associated with the phase transition under the stated conditions.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: All molecules in a thermal sample have the same speed, and a liquid boils at one universal temperature.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What would a molecular speed distribution mean if every molecule had one speed, and why does changing external pressure change the boiling condition?
misconceptions.repair: Keep a distribution of molecular energies, and attach external pressure to any boiling-temperature statement.

exit_task.prompt: Why can evaporation cool a liquid without implying that every molecule had the same initial speed?

answer.summary: Because the sample has a distribution of molecular energies and higher-energy surface molecules can preferentially escape.
reasoning: Removing molecules from the higher-energy tail can lower the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid.
answer.check: Keep the molecular distribution and the surface-vs-bulk distinction explicit.

microtopics.title: Gas-law constraints, mixtures and transport
microtopics.badge_reason: Correct use depends on controlled variables and on separating pressure bookkeeping from effusion-rate comparisons.
entry_assumptions: Can read basic chemical symbols and distinguish a named model from an observation.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac, Avogadro, Dalton and Graham relations answer different conditional questions; the variables and observable must be named before selecting a relation.

teaching_path.action: Name pressure, volume, absolute temperature and amount, then state which variables are fixed.
teaching_path.why_valid: A proportionality is valid only on the constrained path for which it was derived.

teaching_path.action: Use the ideal-gas equation as a common model for state-variable changes.
teaching_path.why_valid: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, changing one state variable generally requires compensating changes in others.
teaching_path.output: The familiar simple gas laws are conditional cases of the same equation-of-state model.

teaching_path.action: Separate Dalton partial-pressure bookkeeping from Graham effusion-rate comparison.
teaching_path.why_valid: Dalton adds component partial pressures in an ideal mixture; Graham compares transport rates under its effusion assumptions.
teaching_path.output: Molar mass belongs in the rate comparison, not in the ideal partial-pressure sum.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any familiar gas-law proportion can be used when several supposedly fixed variables are also changing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If temperature and volume both change, can a fixed-temperature Boyle-law relation alone determine the final pressure?
misconceptions.repair: Write the constraints first and use the combined or ideal-gas model when more than one state variable changes.

exit_task.prompt: Why does Graham's law not justify assigning a larger partial pressure to a lighter gas solely because it has lower molar mass?

answer.summary: Because Graham's law concerns effusion rate, while ideal partial pressure is determined by the component amount, temperature and volume.
reasoning: Molar mass enters the transport-rate relation rather than the Dalton pressure sum.
answer.check: Name the observable—state pressure or transport rate—before selecting the law.

microtopics.title: Real-gas deviations and critical behaviour
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must treat van der Waals terms as state-model corrections and distinguish critical behaviour from ordinary boiling.
entry_assumptions: Can read basic chemical symbols and distinguish a named model from an observation.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Real-gas deviations matter when neglected finite-size and intermolecular-interaction effects are no longer small; equation-of-state corrections do not uniquely specify a microscopic mechanism.

teaching_path.action: Use compressibility factor as a comparison with the ideal reference at the same state.
teaching_path.why_valid: Deviation has meaning relative to a pressure-temperature state and an ideal reference.
teaching_path.output: Z = 1 is the ideal reference; the sign and size of deviation depend on conditions.

teaching_path.action: Interpret van der Waals attraction and excluded-volume terms as phenomenological corrections.
teaching_path.why_valid: Attractions and finite molecular size affect the pressure-volume relation differently and with state-dependent importance.
teaching_path.output: The corrected equation is a thermodynamic model, not a literal collision or bonding mechanism.

teaching_path.action: Distinguish a critical point from an ordinary boiling point.
teaching_path.why_valid: The critical point terminates liquid-vapour coexistence; above the critical temperature compression alone cannot create a separate liquid phase.
teaching_path.output: Liquefaction claims require the temperature-pressure regime to be stated.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A van der Waals equation proves the exact molecular collision mechanism and gives one universal direction of deviation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does an equation of state uniquely determine how molecules collide, and can attraction and finite-size effects dominate equally at every pressure and temperature?
misconceptions.repair: Treat the correction parameters as state-model terms and interpret deviations only with the stated thermodynamic conditions.

exit_task.prompt: Why must a liquefaction statement distinguish critical temperature from boiling temperature?

answer.summary: Boiling temperature is pressure-dependent phase equilibrium below the critical point, while the critical temperature marks whether a distinct liquid-vapour boundary can exist.
reasoning: Boiling is a coexistence condition at a specified pressure.
The critical point terminates that coexistence curve.
answer.check: State which temperature concept is being used and the associated pressure or phase condition.

questions.stem: Why can water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude than near sea level?
conditions: Use the model assumptions and scope stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Lower external pressure lets the vapour-pressure equality required for boiling be reached at a lower temperature.
reasoning: Boiling occurs when the liquid's vapour pressure matches the external pressure.
At high altitude the external pressure is lower, so the equality is reached at a lower temperature.
answer.check: The explanation must use pressure equilibrium rather than a change in water's chemical identity.

questions.stem: A fixed amount of ideal gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
conditions: Use the model assumptions and scope stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Its pressure doubles in the ideal-gas model.
reasoning: Under this isothermal constraint pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
Halving the volume therefore doubles the pressure.
answer.check: Verify that pressure times volume is unchanged between the two states.

difficulty.basis: Single-concept authored Core1A worked anchor after the construction is visible.

questions.stem: Why are real-gas deviations generally more important at high pressure than at sufficiently low pressure?
conditions: Use the model assumptions and scope stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: At high pressure molecules are closer together, so finite molecular size and intermolecular interactions become less negligible relative to ideal assumptions.
reasoning: The ideal model neglects molecular volume and intermolecular forces.
Closer average separation makes those neglected effects comparatively more important.
answer.check: Identify the neglected ideal assumptions without claiming every gas deviates in the same direction.
